items.text: Howard Marks: Scrutinize AI-linked IG and HY exposure; recognize that AI debt now constitutes roughly 12% of the Bloomberg USD IG Corporate index.
Howard Marks: Stress-test portfolios for AI concentration, given that 42 AI-related companies generated around two-thirds of S&P 500 gains since January 2024.
Howard Marks: Assess data-center credits for lease "out clauses," chip collateral durability, and circular transaction linkages before extending exposure.
Howard Marks: Watch whether rate-insensitive AI borrowers elevate government borrowing costs, altering the macro rate backdrop.
Howard Marks: Adopt calibrated humility in AI allocations: size positions small, diversify across predictability tiers, and demand price discipline rather than betting on binary outcomes.
Howard Marks: Treat the early-August move as evidence of sentiment-driven volatility; do not infer fundamentals from daily prices without confirming data.
Howard Marks: Review the global book for crowded levered or carry-related exposures and for correlation assumptions that may fail in a rapid unwind.
Howard Marks: The memo makes no Indonesia-specific claim; keep the IDR book separate and avoid importing global risk-off conclusions without local fundamental checks.
Howard Marks: Stress-test for contagion and “all correlations go to 1” conditions, including forced-selling channels and concentration in volatile psychology-driven moves.
Howard Marks: Use the Mr. Market framework: sell into euphoria and buy into fear only with documented independent valuation, not emotion or formula.
Howard Marks: Treat macro forecasts, including Fed rate-cut and election views, as scenarios with probabilities rather than certainties; check assumptions before sizing positions.
Howard Marks: Review North book exposures that rely on a specific Fed path or election outcome; stress-test for no cuts, delayed cuts, or market reaction diverging from fundamentals.
Howard Marks: Apply the same humility to Indonesia and IDR macro and policy forecasts; avoid assuming Fed spillovers or political outcomes will follow consensus.
Howard Marks: Challenge language and models that imply certainty; ensure risk limits and liquidity plans do not depend on one macro forecast being right.
Howard Marks: Remember past winners can be lucky; double-check conclusions and proceed with caution rather than extrapolating recent success.

Howard Marks: Use Marks’s psychological checklist—irrational exuberance, FOMO, ‘no price too high’—alongside valuation data to monitor global risk appetite; track S&P p/e, top-seven concentration, and AI enthusiasm as sentiment indicators.

Howard Marks: Review USD book exposure to U.S. mega-cap concentration and any assumptions of leader persistence; the memo notes only Microsoft from today’s Magnificent Seven was in the top twenty 24 years earlier.

Howard Marks: Flag concentration and bubble-thinking language as risk indicators; stress-test for multiple compression, remembering Marks cites historical ten-year returns of plus 2% to minus 2% when starting p/e was around today’s 22.
Howard Marks: Present the memo as balanced, not a definitive bubble call: it lists cautionary signs and counterarguments and says Marks cannot speak authoritatively about whether a bubble exists.
Howard Marks: The memo contains no Indonesia or IDR analysis; do not infer a direct South book action from it.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Register Marks's 'sea change' rate thesis as the backdrop: credit expected returns are described as much higher than in 2009-21 and closer to equity returns.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Consider researching a credit allocation program in the USD book, with roughly 7% public / 10% private cited as the relevant return range, and implement only partially per his advice.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): The memo contains no Indonesia or IDR-specific content; treat it as a global framework note and do not extrapolate the 7-10% credit yields to the South book without local data.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Check that the book's absolute risk level is a consciously targeted input to allocation rather than an unintended output of return-seeking, and that it sits 'neither too much nor too little.'

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Remember the optimization-not-maximization framing: define the offense/defense balance first, then treat asset-class, geography and quality choices as implementation details.
Howard Marks: Track U.S. policy proposals on tariffs, price controls, housing subsidies and taxes as potential inflation, fiscal and supply-side risks; the memo argues they carry second-order costs.
Howard Marks: Treat broad tariff and anti-gouging or rent-control proposals as possible consumer-price and regulatory pressures for U.S. exposures; no specific sectors or trades are named.
Howard Marks: Remember that price controls and regulation can distort supply/demand and create shortages or reduced investment; monitor second-order consequences rather than headline intent.
Howard Marks: The document does not analyse Indonesia or emerging markets; no direct South book action follows from it.
Howard Marks: No direct trade or valuation signal is given; use the memo as background for policy-risk discussions rather than as a positioning recommendation.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Log the memo's fiscal points as a long-horizon, not near-term, framework: deficits in 41 of 45 years, $1.8 trillion / 6.4% of GDP in FY2024, interest above defense, and Social Security exhaustion projected for 2035. Do not convert these into a timing signal.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): When assessing tariff-driven inflation, use Marks's distinction between targeted and broad tariffs and his point that domestic producers may raise prices under the umbrella of higher import prices — check whether such increases are appearing rather than assuming tariffs are absorbed abroad.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): The California insurance case is a supply-withdrawal lesson: regulation that caps price without allowing forward-looking risk pricing led to insurer exits and a concentrated state-backed FAIR Plan, with solvency concerns noted. Flag any book exposure where price is set below risk and supply can leave.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): The memo does not discuss Indonesia or the South book. Treat the tariff and price-control arguments as general framework only; no South-specific action follows from this document.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Record the memo's own conclusion — free markets produce imperfect outcomes but efforts to significantly control them make things worse — as a philosophical input, not an asset-price view; stance is n/a.

Howard Marks: Treat the tariff path as unknowable rather than forecastable; build scenarios for retaliation/escalation versus rollback, remembering that negative effects are likely immediate while gains are long-run.

Howard Marks: Review USD book exposure to import-cost inflation, demand destruction, recession risk and Treasury/dollar funding assumptions; the memo questions continued foreign demand for Treasurys but reaches no conclusion.
Howard Marks: The memo contains no Indonesia-specific analysis; do not infer one. Check only verified internal exposures to global trade disruption, USD funding and risk-off credit spreads.

Howard Marks: Scrutinize no-action as an active decision; require probability confidence around any forecast and stress liquidity and credit-spread marks against higher default fear and wider spreads.
Howard Marks: Avoid certainty; if acting on credit bargains, stage entries and document rationale, consistent with Marks’s view that inaction must be judged like action.
Howard Marks: Track whether high yield spreads near 290 bps remain adequate to offset default losses; the memo’s key test is total return, not historical spread levels.

Howard Marks: Review credit allocations across high yield, senior loans, mezzanine, asset-backed loans, CLOs and private lending; the author favors increasing credit and combining public and private exposure.
Howard Marks: Do not infer an IDR or Indonesia credit view from this USD-focused memo; treat it as a global credit framework and require separate local analysis.

Howard Marks: Monitor private credit managers for relaxed credit standards, mark-to-market limitations, forbearance and possible leverage layers; the memo says flaws may appear only when the tide goes out.
Howard Marks: Remember narrow spreads are not synonymous with sub-par medium-to-long-term performance; hold-to-maturity contractual returns can offset temporary spread widening.
Howard Marks: Weigh credit against equities on expected total return and contractual certainty, not only on whether spreads are historically tight.
Howard Marks: Use the ability-versus-willingness risk matrix explicitly when framing portfolio risk capacity; the memo treats this as a core governance decision.
Howard Marks: Avoid treating peer outperformance in a bull market as proof of skill; the memo says a full cycle including good and bad times is needed to distinguish skill from risk bias.
Howard Marks: Do not directly import the U.S. pension plan’s leverage and illiquidity conclusions; the memo describes positions for a specific well-funded plan with a strong sponsor.
Howard Marks: Separate volatility from permanent loss in risk reporting, while recognizing that volatility can be a real constraint for investors with contribution or draw needs.
Howard Marks: When assessing performance, remember the memo’s warning that short-term relative standards are flawed and that the assessment period should cover both good and bad markets.
Howard Marks: Do not build the desk’s process around macro forecasts; Marks repeatedly argues they are seldom helpful and that knowing today’s environment matters more.
Howard Marks: Treat risk as a range of possible outcomes rather than volatility, and check leverage against asset volatility and the holder’s staying power.
Howard Marks: Favor consistent, risk-controlled return profiles and avoidance of poor years over swinging for occasional brilliance; in credit, fewer losers generally serves best.
Howard Marks: When the investing environment changes fundamentally, review strategy thoroughly; the memo cites the 2022 rate sea change as such a case.
Howard Marks: Evaluate managers on long records of consistent, possibly modest outperformance rather than occasional flashes of brilliance.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Treat this as a de-risking prompt rather than a sell signal: the memo explicitly says overvaluation never means 'sure to go down soon.' Consider an INVESTCON 5 posture — pause new aggressive additions and tilt the book toward defensive holdings.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Review U.S. equity exposure against the specific markers cited: forward p/e ~23 at end-2024, price/sales above 3.3x, market cap/GDP at a record, and a 493-stock average p/e of 22. Check how much of North's return depends on the Magnificent Seven (about one-third of index market value).

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Log the memo's crowding indicators — the Barclays 'equity-euphoria indicator' at twice normal, meme-stock attention, and credit yield spreads near all-time lows — as evidence of elevated risk tolerance, and note that many current investors have never worked through a prolonged bear market.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): The memo does not analyse Indonesia; do not extrapolate. Use it only as a sentiment input, and note the caveat that thin credit spreads mean credit's prospective returns are less generous relative to risk-free assets than in history.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Remember the memo's own hedge: 'it's different this time' is usually a bull-market cliché but occasionally true, and Marks says he does not know which applies to AI today. Do not let a valuation-based caution harden into a timing conviction.

Howard Marks: Track U.S. inflation and interest-rate developments; the memo calls rising rates the biggest risk and says inflation’s course is uncertain, while advising preparation rather than forecasting.

Howard Marks: Review duration exposure: Marks says bonds with maturities much above ten years are obvious candidates for underweighting and inflation beneficiaries should be considered for overweighting.
Howard Marks: No Indonesia or IDR-specific claims appear in the memo; treat it as U.S. rate and inflation context only and avoid reading a direct South signal into it.

Howard Marks: Monitor the market-temperature signs the memo lists—speculative and meme stocks, retail/options/margin buying, weak bond protections and elevated IPO activity—while keeping risk posture normal with modest defense.
Howard Marks: Remember the memo explicitly declines a high-conviction top call; do not convert it into an aggressive de-risking instruction.
Warren E. Buffett: Remember Buffett explicitly says expected 2019 equity purchases are not a market call; do not turn the letter into a macro directional signal.
Warren E. Buffett: Use the letter’s quality-business framework—durable economics, sensible price and retained earnings—while noting high private-market prices favor marketable equities.
Warren E. Buffett: The document contains no Indonesia-specific content; do not infer South book actions from Berkshire’s U.S.-centric letter.
Warren E. Buffett: Check liquidity and insurance tail risks: Berkshire pledges at least $20 billion of cash equivalents and warns a mega-catastrophe or cyber event could cause very big losses.
Warren E. Buffett: Focus on operating earnings and intrinsic value, treat repurchases as value-accretive only below intrinsic value, and ignore quarterly GAAP equity mark swings.
Warren E. Buffett: Separate the $29 billion tax-code gain from operating gains when comparing 2017 Berkshire results; do not treat it as recurring.
Warren E. Buffett: Use the letter’s all-equity, no-synergy acquisition framework as a check on high-price, cheap-debt deal assumptions in the North book.

Warren E. Buffett: Flag that GAAP net income can swing with unrealized equity marks; monitor normalized earning power and liquidity, and remember p/c float cannot be withdrawn but catastrophe losses can be large.
Warren E. Buffett: No Indonesia-specific data appears in the document; avoid direct read-across from U.S. tax, insurance and acquisition conditions to the South book.
Warren E. Buffett: Remember the bet’s lesson: low-cost index exposure and low leverage over long horizons; avoid unnecessary activity and fee layers.

Ben Inker and John Pease: Add the U.S. equity-supply calendar to the macro watchlist: SpaceX lockup release on June 12, 2027, Anthropic/OpenAI IPOs, and hyperscaler issuance.

Ben Inker and John Pease: Stress-test North's U.S. equity exposure against GMO's scenario of returns roughly 20% below average over 12-18 months from supply alone, treating the 4x multiplier as an estimate.
Ben Inker and John Pease: Monitor flow sensitivity and liquidity: GMO argues constrained, benchmark-aware and passive markets have fewer opportunistic buyers to absorb new supply.
Ben Inker and John Pease: Remember GMO's catalyst is a hypothesis; verify issuance data and do not present the 20% estimate as guaranteed.
Ben Inker and John Pease: Treat this as a risk/reward shift, not an arbitrage signal; avoid assuming the market can absorb each supply round without a hiccup.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Treat the August–September 2026 Treasury buyback expansion as cosmetic, not a regime change: the memo's list of rate drivers (3.7% PCE, oil/Iran, ~6% deficit, ~$2tn net issuance, AI capex) argues against forecasting a durable decline in long-end yields.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Do not sell U.S. equities on this memo alone — Marks explicitly says the problem is fiscal and dollar-related, not a problem with U.S. companies, and that non-U.S. alternatives carry their own growth, scale and regulation risks.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Flag the 'debasement trade' and the FT's point that Treasury yield suppression may weaken the dollar: review IDR/USD exposure and whether dollar-denominated assets in the South book are truly a hedge or the same risk in another form.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Remember that diversification away from the dollar is not costless and may look wrong for a long time, since no one knows whether or when the fiscal issue comes to a head; size any non-dollar or gold allocation accordingly and note the memo's caveat that no other currency is clearly a substitute.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Keep the memo's asymmetry in mind: an acute event (failed auction, buyers' strike) is judged improbable, while the cost is chronic and already being imposed — so monitor 30-year yields as an ongoing drag on valuation rather than a single tail event.

Lucas White: Remember the letter's claim that energy is the foundation of the economy and that countries leading the electricity race gain a massive edge in AI; track electricity demand, price and grid-investment data as macro inputs.

Lucas White: Review the USD book for indirect exposure to the letter's themes—U.S. natural gas/LNG, uranium, grid equipment, storage and copper—while noting the letter is thematic research, not a security recommendation.

Lucas White: Check the Indonesia book against the letter's point that emerging-market demand revolves more around economic development and infrastructure expansion; assess relevance of grid buildout and commodity demand.

Lucas White: Note the letter's grid-reliability example—the Spain/Portugal outage that left over 50 million people without electricity for almost 20 hours—and consider reliability and concentration risks in energy-transition exposure.

Lucas White: Treat the thesis as secular and long-dated: the letter says natural gas turbines are sold out for years and a nuclear project may take a decade, and it asks investors to sift through neglected areas.

Tina Vandersteel (GMO, Head of Emerging Country Debt): Log GMO's view that the dollar is rich versus EM currencies and that local rates plus cheap FX price many markets to SOFR + 3% — a stance to track, not to adopt without the desk's own valuation work.

Tina Vandersteel (GMO, Head of Emerging Country Debt): The IDR book sits in the local currency EMD universe GMO describes as unusually well valued on rates and FX; check whether current South positioning is consistent with that claim or deliberately differs, and note the document names no country or issuer specifics.

Tina Vandersteel (GMO, Head of Emerging Country Debt): Note the contrast between local currency (cheap currencies, high rates) and hard currency credit (narrow aggregate spreads); any USD EM credit exposure should be judged issue by issue rather than on index-level spread.

Tina Vandersteel (GMO, Head of Emerging Country Debt): Record the implementation risks the letter itself flags: a SOFR + 3% hurdle points to BB and below credit, 3-4 year duration, and possible shorting or credit protection — plus tracking error and peer dispersion for benchmark-agnostic mandates.

Tina Vandersteel (GMO, Head of Emerging Country Debt): Treat this as a framework memo, not a trade idea: it argues total return versus benchmark-relative mandates, so it is relevant to how Six South sets objectives and benchmarks rather than to any single position.
Howard Marks: Distinguish private credit from direct lending and treat low reported volatility in private loans as not equivalent to low credit risk.
Howard Marks: Review any direct lending, BDC, semi-liquid vehicle, or software-related credit exposure for redemption terms, NAV assumptions, leverage, and software concentration.
Howard Marks: Track private credit and private equity stress as part of the broader credit cycle, especially refinancing, coverage ratios, exits, and distributions.
Howard Marks: Remember the memo’s discipline argument: resist fads and do not assume recent direct lending success will persist without a credit cycle.
Howard Marks: No Indonesia-specific claim appears in the memo; use it as a global credit-sentiment input rather than a direct IDR catalyst.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Keep AI exposure moderate and selective per Marks's advice; distinguish proven cash-generative hyperscalers from pre-revenue pure plays and note that the memo calls the latter 'lottery tickets'. Do not treat the demand-growth argument as a valuation argument.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Add two checks to the AI book: (1) how much of AI-linked revenue is circular between AI companies rather than end-user paid, and (2) the pipeline of announced infrastructure build-out, since Claude's supply-shortage case ignores it.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Track AI adoption speed and labor-substitution evidence as a macro variable, including the memo's point that AI's pace of change may exceed society's ability to adjust; treat displaced knowledge work as a demand and policy risk channel.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): When AI-generated research enters the process, require a reasonableness check: the memo notes AI is weaker on genuinely unprecedented situations, can hallucinate confidence, has a limited context window, and carries an explicit 'double check responses' warning.

Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management): Review holdings with labor-heavy, structured-analytical cost bases (software, legal, consulting-type models) for substitution risk, and remember Marks's claim that readily available quantitative information no longer offers an edge that AI cannot match.
Howard Marks: Review AI and data-center exposure for concentration, circular counterparties, SPV or off-balance-sheet leverage, and asset-obsolescence assumptions.
Howard Marks: Avoid all-in or all-out AI positioning; keep exposure moderate and selective, and distinguish equity participation in winner-take-most outcomes from debt exposure.
Howard Marks: Use Marks’s framework to separate company-level speculation from investor psychology, and document bubble criteria rather than relying on labels.
Howard Marks: Remember that the memo offers no definitive bubble verdict; monitor whether enthusiasm becomes irrational without claiming retrospective certainty.
Howard Marks: Treat the memo as US AI-market analysis; do not map its conclusions to the Indonesia book without local evidence.

Howard Marks: Treat recent credit failures as a reminder of clustered credit risk; monitor sub-investment-grade and private-credit exposures for fraud/default indicators without assuming systemic contagion, since Marks calls the issues systematic, not systemic.

Howard Marks: Review North credit holdings for private-credit liquidity mismatch and the First Brands red flags—opaque structures, extensive off-balance-sheet financing, receivables factoring, weak controls—and favor public debt where exit liquidity matters, all else equal.
Howard Marks: Balance deploying capital with prudence; require credit analysis to be a mosaic of inferences and act early on negative conclusions rather than waiting for market consensus.

Howard Marks: Remember defaults are normal and spreads compensate credit risk; do not extrapolate one or two bankruptcies into a broad sub-investment-grade or private-credit thesis, but note Marks’s view that 16 good years may yield more credit surprises.

Howard Marks: No Indonesia-specific claim appears in the memo; do not mechanically map US private-credit episodes to the South book, but keep South credit underwriting standards and fraud checks explicit.

Warren E. Buffett: Remember Buffett’s warning that paper money can lose value if fiscal folly prevails and that fixed-coupon bonds provide no protection against runaway currency; monitor currency and fiscal risk accordingly.
Warren E. Buffett: Use the letter’s stated preference for good businesses over cash-equivalent assets as a reminder not to over-weight cash solely because Berkshire’s cash position draws commentary.
Warren E. Buffett: Check insurance-like exposures for long-tail loss risk and pricing discipline; the document says Berkshire must never write inadequately-priced policies to stay in the game.
Warren E. Buffett: Note the imminent CEO succession to Greg Abel; the document says Abel shares Berkshire’s creed that a report is owed to owners and warns against fooling shareholders.

Warren E. Buffett: Remember the Japan holdings are described as very long term and supported by fixed-rate yen borrowings intended to approximate currency-neutrality; 2025 expected dividend income is about $812 million versus about $135 million interest cost.
Warren E. Buffett: Use Berkshire’s stated rule as a portfolio check: never risk permanent loss of capital, and stress-test liquidity to avoid forced selling.
Warren E. Buffett: Assess North equity holdings on operating earnings and business quality rather than headline GAAP net income, which can swing with unrealized gains and losses.
Warren E. Buffett: Remember Berkshire’s own size and competition warning: expect only modest relative outperformance and do not extrapolate historical eye-popping returns.
Warren E. Buffett: Note the succession clarity: Buffett says Greg Abel is in all respects ready to be CEO of Berkshire tomorrow.

Warren E. Buffett: Do not read Berkshire’s Japanese trading-house position as an Indonesia signal; the letter says outside the U.S. there are essentially no meaningful candidates for Berkshire capital deployment.
Warren E. Buffett: Treat near-term macro forecasting as low-value; the letter says near-term economic and market forecasts are worse than useless and flags huge fiscal deficits as a background issue.
Warren E. Buffett: When assessing US equity earnings, separate operating performance from GAAP mark-to-market swings, as the letter warns GAAP can misinform investors.
Warren E. Buffett: Remember the liquidity stance: hold ample cash and Treasury bills and avoid behavior that creates uncomfortable cash needs in panics or severe insurance losses.
Warren E. Buffett: Favor long-term business quality and value-accretive capital allocation; the letter rejects short-term trading and warns that overpaid buybacks hurt continuing shareholders.
